text: The same ancilla-CNOT-measure primitive from Chapter 3, scaled up to a full 2D lattice — plus one genuinely new wrinkle that small codes didn't force you to confront.

Each surface-code ancilla sits at the center of one lattice face and entangles to its up to 4 neighboring data qubits via CNOT or CZ gates — structurally the identical idea as Lesson 13's 2-CNOT circuit, just with up to 4 CNOTs matching the surface code's 4-qubit stabilizers. The ancilla is then measured, and that bit is the stabilizer's syndrome for this round. Because every stabilizer has its own dedicated ancilla, this runs in parallel across the whole lattice — every ancilla prepared, entangled, and measured in the same timestep, which is what makes the surface code practical on real hardware with many qubits operating simultaneously.

Here's the new wrinkle: a faulty ancilla measurement can't be treated as a minor footnote, because the surface code is built to protect a logical qubit continuously, for as long as a computation runs. The fix is to run many rounds of syndrome extraction in a row and track how each stabilizer's value changes over time. A real data error flips a stabilizer's outcome and keeps it flipped in every subsequent round until corrected. A faulty ancilla measurement typically causes an isolated flip in just one round, reverting back to normal the next round. Looking at the pattern across time, not any single round, is what lets a decoder tell these two situations apart.

This turns syndrome data three-dimensional: two spatial dimensions, the lattice, plus one time dimension, the round number. A triggered stabilizer outcome that persists across rounds is thought of as a defect, which must be paired up with another defect, or with the lattice boundary, to identify the most likely underlying error chain.
That pairing problem is exactly the decoding problem the next lesson addresses: turning a lattice full of flipped and unflipped stabilizer outcomes into an actual correction, fast enough to matter.
